meta.title: How Large Language Models Work
meta.thesis: A large language model works by tokenizing visible text, building contextual vectors with transformer attention, scoring possible next tokens, and decoding one token at a time until the response stops.

mentalMap.title: How LLMs Work — from text to next token
mentalMap.caption: Each step explains one mechanism a beginner needs before debugging model behavior.
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: An LLM repeatedly turns visible tokens into next-token probabilities; everything else is packaging, decoding, and validation around that loop.

nodes.label: Text becomes tokens
nodes.sub: Build the simplest useful picture of How Large Language Models Work.
nodes.what: Tokenization is the boundary where human text becomes model input IDs.
nodes.relevance: It explains why long prompts, code, and non-English text can consume context unexpectedly.
nodes.orient: How raw text is split into model-specific pieces before any reasoning happens.

nodes.label: Tokens enter context
nodes.sub: See the moving parts and how they interact.
nodes.what: Embeddings and context windows are the model’s visible workspace.
nodes.relevance: They explain why missing or truncated evidence cannot influence the answer.
nodes.orient: How token vectors and the context window define what the model can use.

nodes.label: Attention mixes evidence
nodes.sub: Make the choices that change quality, cost, or risk.
nodes.what: Attention builds contextual token states from the visible sequence.
nodes.relevance: It explains why wording and position change model behavior.
nodes.orient: How transformer layers let each position use nearby and distant token information.

nodes.label: Logits become words
nodes.sub: Connect the concept to a small practical artifact.
nodes.what: Decoding turns raw scores into the next visible token.
nodes.relevance: It explains variability, repetition, and why low temperature is not truth.
nodes.orient: How next-token scores, temperature, and sampling produce the response stream.

nodes.label: Fluent can be false
nodes.sub: Use active recall and a decision checklist to make it stick.
nodes.what: Failure modes follow directly from the prediction loop.
nodes.relevance: It tells learners what to check before trusting an answer.

modules.title: Text becomes tokens
modules.sub: Start with the boundary between human text and model input.
modules.summary: A model does not see words; it sees token IDs produced by a tokenizer. This module makes tokenization concrete before introducing any transformer machinery.
objectives: Explain why tokens are not the same as words.
Predict why code, tables, or multilingual text can fill context quickly.
Use tokenization to debug a prompt that unexpectedly truncates.

blocks.title: The model reads token IDs, not sentences

spans.text: A large language model begins with a tokenizer. The tokenizer maps text into token IDs, and the model operates on those IDs. Some tokens are whole words, some are word pieces, and some are whitespace or punctuation.
Problem anchor: a product manager asks why a long support ticket ignored the JSON instruction at the top. The first check is not “is the model smart?” It is “what tokens actually reached the model?”
Before reading on, predict: which usually costs more tokens, a short English sentence or a dense code snippet with punctuation and indentation?

blocks.analogy: Tokenization is like cutting a document into puzzle pieces before handing it to a reader; odd cuts change what fits in the box.

blocks.title: Worked token budget: the refund ticket

spans.text: Imagine a prompt with system rules, a 4,000-word support ticket, and a JSON schema at the top. The model can only condition on the packed context window.

items.text: The app builds the prompt: rules first, ticket second, schema third.
The tokenizer splits the ticket, timestamps, invoice IDs, and quoted emails into many small pieces.
If the request is over budget, the packer drops or summarizes older content.
If the schema is dropped or buried, the model may answer fluently but miss the required shape.

spans.text: The fix is mechanical: measure token budget, keep durable instructions near the final task, and validate the output rather than trusting the prose.

blocks.title: Check tokenization
blocks.prompt: Why can a prompt lose an important instruction even when the user pasted it?

options.text: Because LLMs ignore all instructions before user text.
Because the instruction may be outside the packed context or buried behind too many tokens.
Because tokenization converts every word into a fixed one-word token.

blocks.explanation: The model only conditions on what fits in the current token window; token boundaries and packing decide what survives.

modules.title: Embeddings and the context window
modules.sub: After text is tokenized, the model embeds only the visible tokens.
modules.summary: Token IDs become vectors, and the context window is the model’s working input, not durable memory.
objectives: Describe what an embedding does at inference time.
Distinguish context from memory or knowledge.
Spot when missing context explains a bad answer.

blocks.title: Token IDs become vectors in a limited workspace

spans.text: Each token ID is mapped to a learned vector before transformer layers process it. The vector itself is not a fact database. It is the starting representation the network will update using surrounding context.
The context window is the visible workspace for one request. If a customer policy, tool result, or schema is not in that workspace, the model cannot directly attend to it.
Recall from module 1: if a schema disappears from the packed prompt, what kind of failure should you expect?

blocks.analogy: Embeddings are like name tags that give each token a starting position before the room starts a discussion.

blocks.title: Case study: the missing policy paragraph

spans.text: A support assistant answers: “Refunds after 35 days are allowed.” The real policy says refunds must arrive within 30 days, but that paragraph was summarized away.

items.text: What did not fail: the model produced fluent text.
What failed: the relevant evidence was absent from the context window.
Decision: fix packing or retrieval before changing model temperature or fine-tuning.

blocks.title: Check context
blocks.prompt: What is the safest interpretation of “the model forgot the policy”?

options.text: The model deleted the policy from its weights.
The policy probably was not in the current context, or it was compressed badly.
The tokenizer refused to encode policy text.

blocks.explanation: For a single request, “forgetting” usually means missing, stale, or poorly packed context.

modules.title: Attention builds contextual states
modules.sub: Visible token vectors then exchange information through attention layers.
modules.summary: Attention lets token positions weight other visible positions, creating context-aware states used for prediction.
objectives: Connect position and wording to model behavior.
Predict why long contexts can still miss the salient fact.

blocks.title: Attention asks which visible tokens matter now

spans.text: Inside transformer layers, each token position compares with other visible positions. Attention weights decide how much information to mix from those positions into the current state.
This is why the same fact can matter more or less depending on where it appears, how clearly it is labeled, and what the current token is trying to predict.
Attention is powerful, but it is not a guarantee of faithful evidence use. It can connect tokens; it cannot make absent evidence present.

blocks.analogy: Attention is like highlighting parts of an open notebook while writing the next word; closed pages cannot be highlighted.

blocks.title: One prediction pass through the model
blocks.caption: Click through the mechanism that turns visible tokens into a next-token state.

steps.label: Compare positions
steps.detail: Queries and keys produce attention scores.

steps.label: Mix values
steps.detail: Weighted values update each token state.

steps.label: Project logits
steps.detail: The final state scores possible next tokens.

blocks.title: Check attention

options.text: It can retrieve facts that were never sent to the model.
It can weight and mix information from visible tokens when building contextual states.
It can prove that the model used the best evidence faithfully.

blocks.explanation: Attention works over visible context; it does not guarantee truth or retrieval.

modules.title: Logits, sampling, and stopping
modules.sub: The contextual state becomes scores, and decoding chooses the next token.
modules.summary: The model scores possible next tokens; decoding settings choose one and repeat the loop.
objectives: Define logits and decoding in plain language.
Explain what temperature changes and what it does not.
Read a tiny next-token loop as runnable code.

blocks.title: Generation is a loop, not a paragraph lookup

spans.text: At each step, the model projects its final token state into logits: raw scores for every token in the vocabulary. Decoding converts those scores into the next token, appends it, and runs the process again.
Temperature and top-p change how the model chooses among likely continuations. Lower temperature can reduce variety, but it does not verify facts or enforce a schema by itself.

blocks.analogy: Decoding is like choosing the next tile from a weighted bag, placing it, then recalculating the bag for the next move.

blocks.title: Predict a tiny decoder

spans.text: Run this as a tiny model of the mechanism. The point is to predict behavior before trusting the output.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Predict the two printed tokens before revealing.
predictThenReveal.answer:
It prints:
refund
invoice

Greedy decoding picks the highest-scoring token each time. Real sampling can be less deterministic, but it still starts from next-token scores.

syntax.explains: The small concrete case the example operates on.
The line or function that turns the inputs into behavior.
A visible result so you can check your prediction.

blocks.title: How to verify an AI-generated LLM explanation

spans.text: When an AI explains LLMs or writes a toy decoder, check the mechanism rather than the polish.

items.text: Does it show tokenization before attention and decoding?
Does it distinguish context from durable memory?
Does it say temperature changes randomness, not truth?
Does any code actually compute a visible next-token decision?

modules.title: Why fluent answers can be wrong
modules.sub: Finally connect the mechanism to hallucination, truncation, and validation.
modules.summary: A next-token model can produce fluent unsupported text, especially when evidence is missing or decoding rewards plausible continuation.
objectives: Name topic-specific failure modes of LLM generation.
Choose the right fix for missing facts versus malformed output.
Reconstruct the full mechanism from memory.

blocks.title: How the mechanism breaks in practice

spans.text: Fluency is a product of the next-token objective. It is not proof that the answer is grounded. A model can continue in a plausible style even when context is stale, missing, or ambiguous.

items.text: Unsupported claims: the model fills gaps with likely continuations.
Hidden truncation: the instruction or source was outside the packed context.
Schema drift: the response sounds right but violates required fields.
False confidence: low temperature makes wording steadier, not more factual.

blocks.analogy: A fluent LLM answer is like a well-spoken witness; you still need evidence.

spans.text: A JSON extraction prompt fails on long support tickets. The output is prose, not JSON, and the answer includes a policy not present in the ticket.

items.text: If the schema is missing from context: repack the prompt and validate output.
If the policy is missing: use retrieval or a tool, not fine-tuning.
If JSON is malformed: use structured outputs plus a validator.
If the answer is unsupported: require citations or claim-level checks.

blocks.title: Check the full mechanism
blocks.prompt: Which statement best summarizes how an LLM works?

options.text: It retrieves complete answers from a database inside the model.
It predicts one token at a time from visible context, then repeats until stopping.
It checks every claim against the internet before responding.

blocks.explanation: The core interface is next-token prediction conditioned on packed context; grounding and validation must be added around it.

spans.text: From memory, reconstruct the LLM loop: text becomes tokens, tokens become vectors, attention builds contextual states, logits score next tokens, and decoding repeats. Then name two reasons a fluent answer can still be wrong.
